title: References and Pointers
summary: Pass by reference, const references, pointers and nullptr, the arrow operator, the three const pointer forms, and the dangling-reference bug every C++ programmer meets once.
introduction: Every value in C++ lives somewhere in memory, and references and pointers are the two ways to talk about that place instead of copying the value. References give a function access to the caller's variable; pointers can also point at nothing, be re-pointed, and walk through arrays. Knowing which to use, and when neither is needed, is the first skill that separates C++ from the scripting languages. This lesson builds that skill with four short programs.
learningObjectives: Pass arguments by reference and by const reference and explain the difference from pass by value
Declare, dereference and re-point a pointer and test it against nullptr
Read the three const pointer forms correctly
Recognise and avoid dangling references and pointers

blocks.text: References: another name for an object

A reference is declared with `&` after the type and must be initialised with an existing object; from then on it *is* that object under another name. It can never be re-bound or be null. Functions use reference parameters for two reasons: to modify the caller's variable, and to avoid copying something large. For the second case add `const`, which lets the function read but not write.

blocks.title: references.cpp
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra references.cpp -o references
$ ./references
x=2 y=1
x=10
Grace!

blocks.text: If swapValues took plain int inputs, it would only swap copies. References let it change the original values. Use const references when a function should read a large value without copying or changing it. For example, std::sort(v.begin(), v.end()) changes the order of a vector. std::size(v) only reads its size.
Pointers: an address you can inspect

A pointer is a variable that holds the **address** of another object. `&value` produces the address, `int* p` declares a pointer to an `int`, and `*p` (dereferencing) reaches the object at that address. Unlike a reference, a pointer can be changed to point elsewhere and can hold `nullptr`, meaning "points at nothing". Those two abilities are exactly when you want a pointer: optional results and data structures whose links change.

blocks.title: pointers.cpp
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra pointers.cpp -o pointers
$ ./pointers
42
43
7
p is null

blocks.text: Dereferencing a null pointer is undefined behaviour and usually crashes the program with a segmentation fault, so test for `nullptr` before using a pointer that might be empty. Use `nullptr`, never `0` or the C macro `NULL`: `nullptr` has its own type, so it cannot be mistaken for an integer in overload resolution.
Pointers to structs and the arrow operator

A `struct` groups named fields into one type. Through a pointer you reach a field with `->`, shorthand for `(*p).field`. The function below returns a pointer precisely because the answer may not exist; a reference could not express "not found".

blocks.title: find.cpp
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra find.cpp -o find
$ ./find
Linus scored 78
Grace not found

blocks.text: The returned pointer is a `const Student*`: a pointer to a `const` object, so the caller can read the student but not change it. `const` can sit in two places around a pointer, and they mean different things.

The loop variable of a range-based `for` is a fresh copy of each element unless you declare it as a reference. That difference decides whether the loop can modify the container, and for large elements whether it copies them needlessly. `const auto&` is the safe default when you only read.

blocks.title: loopref.cpp
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra loopref.cpp -o loopref
$ ./loopref
doubled copy: 20
doubled copy: 40
doubled copy: 60
10, 20, 30
20, 40, 60

blocks.title: Common mistake: returning a reference to a local variable
blocks.text: `const std::string& makeName() { std::string local{"temp"}; return local; }` compiles, but `local` is destroyed when the function returns, so the caller receives a **dangling reference** to freed memory. Reading it is undefined behaviour and often appears to work until the memory is reused. GCC warns with `reference to local variable 'local' returned [-Wreturn-local-addr]`. The fix is simple: return the `std::string` by value. The same bug exists with pointers (`return &local;`) and with references stored in objects that outlive what they refer to.

rows: Function must see or modify the caller's object
Reference (`T&`, or `const T&` to read only)
Link that changes over time (list nodes, tree children)

blocks.title: Raw pointers do not own anything
blocks.text: In modern C++ a plain `T*` means "I can look at this object but I am not responsible for deleting it". Memory you allocate yourself belongs in a smart pointer; the [smart pointers lesson](/tutorials/cpp/smart-pointers) shows why `new` and `delete` almost never appear in new code.

questions.question: Which statement about references is true?
questions.explanation: A reference must be bound when declared and stays bound to that object for its whole life. Pointers are the ones that can be null or re-pointed.
options: A reference can be re-bound to another object later
A reference must be initialised and cannot be null
A reference holds a copy of the object
A reference needs `*` to read the value
